data.text/markdown:
How much do USGS river gage peaks change between real time and approval?

When a flood crest goes out from a USGS streamgage, the number on the USGS website is provisional. Months later a hydrographer reviews the record and USGS publishes the approved value. Prediction markets such as Polymarket's river-crest markets settle on the provisional number and ignore later revisions, and flood planners read the same live numbers. USGS does not keep the provisional values it showed, so nobody has measured how far they sit from the approved ones (USGS SIR 2017-5137). The Iowa Environmental Mesonet (IEM) has archived the values gages transmitted through NOAA's HADS system since about 2008. This notebook compares, for about 100 flood-prone gages and water years 2009 to the latest approved year, the annual peak gage height as transmitted (IEM) with the approved peak (USGS Water Data OGC API v1, continuous collection), and the same for discharge where IEM has it (a few gages, mostly 2022 onward). IEM holds what the gage sent. USGS can edit values after transmission (delete a spike, apply a datum correction) before or while they show on its website, and those edits may not reach HADS. So "as transmitted" is a proxy for what the website showed, close for most hours but not a copy.

1. Pick the gages

We want gages that flood and that have long IEM archives. A gage is a candidate if IEM's archive for it starts by the end of 2010 (late 2007 in the Midwest states, November 2010 in most others, so those gages cover water years 2011 on), it transmits gage height (HG) as its main variable, and it is an NWS forecast point (HAS_HML). For each of 20 states spread across the country, including the ice-affected north (MN, ND, WI, MI, ME, VT, MT, NY), we shuffle the candidates with a fixed seed and keep the first five that NOAA's NWPS service maps to a USGS gage with a minor flood stage. We add the gages the question names: the White River at Indianapolis (03353000, the settled Polymarket market) and the two Helene gages near Asheville (03451500 French Broad, 03451000 Swannanoa), whose IEM archive starts in December 2010.

data.text/markdown:
2. Find each year's flood windows

Pulling a full year of 15-minute values from both sources takes about five minutes per gage-year from IEM, so we pull only the days that matter. For each gage we read USGS's approved daily means (gage height, or discharge where USGS publishes no daily stage), and for each water year take the three highest days at least five days apart. Around each of those days we pull a three-day window of 15-minute values from both USGS (approved and provisional, with qualifiers) and IEM (as transmitted). The annual peak on each side is the highest value across the same three windows, so both sides look at exactly the same hours. The catch: a transmitted spike on a day that isn't among the approved top three is missed. Section 6 checks how often that happens with full-year pulls for a sample of gage-years.

data.text/markdown:
3. Compare peaks, gage-year by gage-year

IEM stores each SHEF series under a code. Gage height is HG… and discharge is QR… (in thousands of cfs). Where a gage sends more than one HG series (primary and backup sensor) we take the one it reports most often. A gage-year counts as approved only if every USGS value in its windows is approved. For each gage-year we record the approved peak and its time, the transmitted peak and its time, and the window offset: the median transmitted-minus-approved difference at matching timestamps across the windows. A peak revision close to the window offset means USGS shifted the whole record (a datum or gage-height correction); a peak revision much larger than it means the peak itself was edited (a spike removed, a gap filled, ice). The HADS feed also carries garbage readings: a 1,213 ft stage at a gage that never tops 30 ft, from a garbled radio message. USGS's website doesn't show those, so before taking the transmitted peak we drop any reading more than 1 ft (and more than 10%) away from the median of its five-reading neighbourhood (25% and 500 cfs for discharge), and any reading more than 25% and 2 ft above the highest value USGS approved at that gage in any of our windows (garbage often arrives in runs, which the median misses). We count how often such a spike sat above the crest. We also check that the gage transmitted something within two hours of the approved peak, because a transmission gap at the crest makes the "transmitted peak" meaningless rather than revised.

data.text/markdown:
4. Gage height: how big are the revisions?

Before measuring we drop three kinds of gage-year and count them: years not yet fully approved, years with no transmission within two hours of the approved crest, and gages whose transmitted stage sits on a different datum from USGS's gage height across all years (median window offset over 0.3 ft, a NWS-versus- USGS reference difference, not a revision). The flood-category flip counts use the NWS action, minor, moderate and major stages for each gage; a whole-foot flip means the two peaks fall on different sides of an integer foot, the kind of band edge a crest market uses.

data.text/markdown:
5. The worst cases

The fifteen largest gage-height revisions, with what the record says about them. Every gage-year over 0.1 ft gets a cause:
  • USGS has no value at the transmitted crest: the gage sent a higher reading, and the approved record has nothing within an hour of it. USGS deleted those hours, typically for ice, a frozen or failed sensor or a fouled orifice line.
  • whole window shifted: the revision equals the median shift across the windows, a datum or gage-height correction applied to the whole record.
  • crest value changed: USGS kept the hour but published a different value.
We also flag crests in the ice months (December to March).

data.text/markdown:
6. Did the windows miss any transmitted peaks?

For a seeded sample of approved gage-years we pull the whole water year from IEM and check whether the gage's highest transmitted stage (after the same garbage filter) fell inside our three windows. A transmitted maximum outside them is usually a spike or a bad value that USGS removed, which is a revision our window method doesn't count.

data.text/markdown:
7. Discharge, where IEM has it

IEM has transmitted discharge (QR) at only some gages, mostly from 2022 on. Discharge is computed from stage through a rating curve, and USGS revises ratings and applies shifts after field measurements, so we expect larger revisions here than for stage.

data.text/markdown:
What this doesn't show

  • IEM is a proxy for the USGS website. It stores what the gage transmitted through HADS; edits USGS made before or after display don't appear in it.
  • Windows around the approved top three days can miss a transmitted spike elsewhere in the year; section 6 measures how often.
  • The gage sample is NWS forecast points with long IEM archives, not a random sample of all USGS gages.
  • Discharge covers only the gages that transmit it to HADS, mostly 2022 onward.
